Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I have to be on guard all the time
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.explanation: The trigger set mixes a socially evaluative trigger ('being seen') with nonspecific discomfort/detachment, while the threat items center on danger from sudden sounds, home intrusion, and interpersonal harm. For a combat trauma profile, 'being seen' is not impossible, but here it is poorly linked to the stated threat pattern and stands out as the one trigger not plausibly connected to the strong Triggers→Threat and Triggers→Negative Appraisals edges.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilance to loud sounds and watching others for danger fit a combat-related threat profile, but specifically monitoring for someone entering the home implies a domestic intrusion threat context that is not supported by the triggers, memory, or appraisals. It pulls the profile toward a different trauma context and weakens cross-node coherence.

vignette: The afternoon Kwame was deployed to the valley had been thick with dry dust and the sharp scent of diesel exhaust from the Humvees. When the detonation cracked overhead, it was sudden and loud, tearing through the hum of the patrol. He remembered the precise angle of the blast, the way the dust plumed in a sudden, bruised cloud, and the high whine of Chinooks cutting through the smoke. What stayed with him most was the olfactory echo: even now, when he thinks of that day, the sharp tang of burnt fuel and heated earth rises unbidden, mirroring the smells that had been present during the frightening event. His memories of the engagement do not fade like ordinary recollections; they arrive with a clarity that makes them feel more real and vivid than ordinary memories. He can trace every detail-the rustle of gear, the clipped radio calls, the sudden stillness before the orders came. The event sits in his mind not as a past story, but as something that merely paused. In the months after returning to the American Midwest, Kwame found his attention fixed outward. He was certain that unexpected or loud sounds carried a quiet threat, so his posture tightened the moment a car backfired or a door slammed. He watched the people around him closely, reading their faces and movements for any flicker of harm or surprise. While patrolling the trails at his job as a park ranger, his eyes constantly swept the tree line, the parking lots, and the visitor pathways, cataloguing anything that might shift. When an air tour helicopter approached the valley, the familiar rotor beat would meet him in the open. His chest tightened with discomfort, and a quiet, detached unreality settled over him, as if the world had grown slightly out of reach. He had come to believe he must remain on guard all the time, that letting his shoulders drop even for a moment would leave him exposed. As the weeks turned to months, Kwame's cautious routines solidified into habits. He avoided the ridge trails during peak flight hours. The sound consistently met his attention, and his hands would linger on his equipment, double-checking straps and zippers. The inaction guilt he carried from the combat zone coexisted with his daily observations; he kept returning to the memory of those final, breathless seconds, certain he would never forgive himself for not moving faster, for not doing more to stop what happened. He felt permanently changed for the worse, as if a piece of his former ease had been lost to the dust. With his wife, Amara, he learned to watch her carefully, noting how her quiet sighs or sudden movements might signal strain. His constant alertness ran alongside his marriage, and his crew has noticed how he hesitates to delegate tasks, the occupational consequence of his vigilance becoming clear in the quiet gaps between assignments. Now, at forty-six, Kwame stands in the ranger station with the morning light filtering through the pines, his radio crackling with visitor reports. The sound of a maintenance truck reversing pulls his head up, and he feels the old discomfort ripple through him, followed quickly by that familiar sense of detachment. He knows he can no longer sustain the endless watching. His PCL-5 score of thirty-three sits quietly beside his daily reality. What he hopes for is simply to hear the sky without bracing, to let the past stay where it belongs, and to believe, even for an hour, that he is safe exactly as he is. He seeks help as the stillness begins to feel heavier than the alertness, and he fears that if he does not learn to rest without looking away, he will lose what remains of his life in the valley.
